primitives.name: Diversity-Prediction Theorem
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Prediction diversity: δ = (1/N)Σ(g_i - ⟨g⟩)2 (variance of estimates; called "precision" in stats literature).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'g_i': 'Individual estimate (dimensionless)', '\\langle g \\rangle': 'Mean estimate (same units as truth)', 'G': 'True value (ground truth; same units as g_i)', 'N': 'Number of estimates (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: No independence assumptions required; holds exactly for any finite sample.
primitives.breakdown_regime: None; the identity is universally valid.

layer2.mapping: The DPT provides the foundational decomposition for both GSI and GSE uncertainty quantification. In GSI, it underpins the Bayesian posterior variance identity. In GSE, it maps directly to the ensemble calibration diagnostics used for model selection and pruning.
layer2.telemetry: Weekly tracking of δ/ε (fraction of individual MSE canceled by diversity) serves as a redundancy metric for model ensembles.

primitives.name: Collective Error Variance Identity
primitives.verbatim_quote: Equations & assumptions - Quadratic collective error: γ = (⟨g⟩ - G)2.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'γ': 'Quadratic collective error (units squared)', 'G': 'True value (ground truth; same units as g_i)', '\\langle g \\rangle': 'Mean estimate (same units as G)'}
primitives.breakdown_regime: None; the identity is universally valid.

layer2.mapping: In GSI, this is the frequentist analogue of the posterior predictive variance. In GSE, it measures the systematic bias of the ensemble mean.
layer2.telemetry: Tracking γ alongside ε and δ enables detection of persistent calibration shifts.

primitives.name: Individual Error Variance
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Average quadratic individual error: ε = (1/N)Σ(g_i - G)2.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'ε': 'Average individual error variance (units squared)', 'G': 'True value (ground truth; same units as g_i)', 'g_i': 'Individual estimate (dimensionless)', 'N': 'Number of estimates (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Equal weighting of all individual estimates.
primitives.breakdown_regime: None; the identity is universally valid.

layer2.mapping: ε corresponds to the average out-of-sample loss of individual models in GSE, and to the prior variance in GSI.
layer2.telemetry: Baseline ε level indicates the inherent noise in the base forecasters.

primitives.name: Negative Result on Prediction Spread
primitives.verbatim_quote: - The authors' key analytic point: γ = ε - δ does NOT imply increasing δ decreases γ, because ε and δ are not independent — raising diversity can raise individual error unpredictably.
primitives.assumptions: No additional assumptions beyond the DPT itself.
primitives.breakdown_regime: None; the result is a fundamental limitation of the theorem's interpretation.

layer2.mapping: This negative result establishes that prediction spread cannot be used as a direct confidence signal for individual outcomes, even when the crowd average is accurate. It creates a veto condition for using δ as a standalone diagnostic.
layer2.telemetry: If δ increases while ε remains stable or rises, the crowd is becoming less reliable overall, despite potentially unchanged collective accuracy.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that while the diversity-prediction theorem (DPT) guarantees a perfect algebraic decomposition of ensemble error into individual error minus diversity, it does NOT guarantee that maximizing diversity will reduce collective error. This is because the individual error ε itself depends on the diversity δ. If a crowd becomes more diverse, some estimators may start making worse, more idiosyncratic errors, which raises ε. The DPT merely states that the difference ε - δ is constant across any fixed set of estimators, not that one can freely adjust δ to lower the total error. This is a critical failure mode for naive applications of the 'wisdom of crowds' doctrine, where one might try to boost accuracy by artificially increasing disagreement among forecasters.
